readerTitle: How Tylenol grew by talking about aspirin
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Tylenol의 1970년대 광고, Ries & Trout가 소개한 사례) + 가상 적용 (재사용 물류 상자 제조사, 일정 관리 소프트웨어)
insight: 시장 1위의 강점을 이길 수 없다면, 그 강점에 숨은 비용을 고객에게 보여주어 1위가 고객 머릿속에서 차지한 자리를 바꾼다.
misconception: 경쟁에서 이기려면 우리 제품의 장점을 더 크게 외치거나 가격을 낮춰야 한다. 경쟁사 이야기는 하지 않는 편이 낫다.

sources.text: Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1981). Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. McGraw-Hill. (Repositioning the competition 장, Tylenol 대 aspirin 사례)
재사용 상자 제조사와 일정 관리 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Tylenol 광고 문구("For the millions who should not take aspirin" 계열)는 Ries & Trout의 책에 인용된 내용입니다. 카드에는 직접 인용 대신 요약해 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문 문구와 광고 시기(1970년대)를 다시 확인하세요.
Tylenol이 이후 미국에서 가장 많이 팔리는 진통제 브랜드 중 하나가 되었다는 내용은 Ries & Trout의 서술에 근거합니다. 정확한 1위 달성 시기와 시장점유율 수치는 확인되지 않아 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
Tylenol은 McNeil(Johnson & Johnson 계열) 브랜드입니다. 카드에는 회사명을 쓰지 않고 브랜드명만 썼습니다.
비교 광고 규제는 나라마다 다릅니다. 7번 카드에는 일반적인 주의만 적었고 법률 조언은 하지 않습니다.

cards.title: How Tylenol grew by talking about aspirin
body: In the 1970s, aspirin was the pain reliever almost every home already trusted.
Tylenol's ads chose an odd focus. They spent much of their words not on Tylenol, but on aspirin, and on who perhaps shouldn't take it. That one move changed how many people saw the market leader.

image.label: A spotlight shifting from a big pill bottle to a smaller one
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 무대 위 크고 익숙한 알약 병 하나와 그 옆 작은 병 하나. 조명이 큰 병의 작은 경고 라벨을 비추다가 작은 병 쪽으로 옮겨가는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고, 상표, 포장 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Everyone ships in cardboard.
body: You make reusable plastic crates for food distributors. Almost every buyer uses cardboard boxes. They're cheap and familiar.
Buyers keep saying the same thing: "Your crate costs ten times more than a box." What do you lead with?

options.text: Cut your price to get closer to cardboard
options.feedback: You'll never be as cheap as a box, and you give up margin while still being judged on the box's terms.

options.text: Highlight what your crate does well: strong, stackable, washable
options.feedback: All true, but buyers still see cardboard as the cheap, sensible default. Your features sound like extras they don't need.

options.text: Show what cardboard really costs: bought again every trip, crushed loads, waste to haul away
options.feedback: This changes how buyers see the default itself. "Cheap" starts to look like "paid for again and again." It takes real numbers to be believed.

cards.title: Tylenol made aspirin look different.
body: Aspirin's position was simple: the safe, trusted choice for pain. Tylenol could not out-trust it head-on.
So its ads pointed to a true but little-discussed fact. Aspirin can upset the stomach, and some people are advised to avoid it. The message, roughly: *for the millions who should not take aspirin*.
Aspirin didn't change. How people saw it did. Tylenol went on to become one of America's best-selling pain relievers.

cards.title: Repositioning the competition
body: **Repositioning the competition** means changing how customers see a rival, usually the leader, so there's room for you in their mind.

Al Ries and Jack Trout named the idea in their 1981 book *Positioning*. Their point: when a leader owns a spot in people's minds, you often can't push your way in. First you loosen the idea customers already hold about the leader.

image.label: A leader's strength flipped to show its hidden cost
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 큰 상자에 "Leader: Cheap", 화살표를 따라 뒤집히면 뒷면에 "Bought again every trip". 오른쪽에 작은 상자 "You: Buy once". 깔끔한 플랫 스타일, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three steps, same pattern.
body: The move usually follows the same path:
list: **Find the belief:** what do customers trust the leader for? (*cheap, safe, complete*)
**Find the hidden cost:** what true downside comes with that strength?
**Make the gap yours:** show that your offer is built for exactly that downside
cards.callout: For the crates: cardboard is cheap per box, but you buy it on every trip. A crate is bought once.

cards.title: Small businesses use it too.
body: A local hardware shop faces a huge chain store down the road. The chain owns *low prices, huge range*.
The shop doesn't fight on either. It points to the cost hidden in "huge range": twenty minutes hunting the aisles and no one to ask. Its sign reads: "In and out in five minutes, with advice."
The chain is still cheaper. But for a rushed customer with a leaking tap, it now looks slow.

cards.title: It only works if it's true and it matters.
body: The hidden cost must be real, and something customers care about. Exaggerated claims damage your credibility fast, and rules on comparing yourself to rivals vary by country. Check yours before naming a competitor.
Attacks can also look petty and give the rival free attention. And the leader can reply by fixing the weakness. Keep the focus on the customer's problem, not on mocking the other company.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app.
body: Your app helps small clinics book patients. The big rival is an all-in-one practice suite that clinic owners see as *the complete, serious option*.

options.text: Say the suite is bloated and outdated
options.feedback: It sounds like name-calling. Owners who chose the suite feel insulted, and you've given them no fact to rethink.

options.text: Show the cost of "complete": months of setup and staff training before a single booking
options.feedback: It turns the rival's strength into a real, measurable cost. Your app now looks like the fast choice, not the small one.

options.text: Offer the same features at half the price
options.feedback: Cheaper may win some users, but you accept the suite's frame and race to copy its features.

cards.title: If you can't beat the leader's strength, show its hidden cost.
body: Customers already hold an idea about the leader. Change that idea honestly, and space opens up for you.
**Try it today:** write the one word customers use for your biggest rival. Then list one true cost that comes with it.
